newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - Italy seen firmly in second EMU wave.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Italy seen firmly in second EMU wave.

text.p: Italy is unlikely to squeeze its way into the group of countries founding European currency union, despite Rome's eagerness to join, according to a Reuters survey of economic experts published on Friday.

A poll of the opinions of 45 economists and think tanks across 15 European countries shows that expectations for Italian founder membership of European economic and monetary union (EMU), scheduled for January 1, 1999, are low and waning.
Only three of the 45 economists -- seven percent -- tipped Italy to be in the first EMU wave, down from 17 percent in January and 22 percent in December.
The figures are bad news for Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, who meets Helmut Kohl on Friday in a bid to assure the German Chancellor that Italy is fit to join the EMU club from the launch.

"It is going to be very difficult for Italy to join EMU in the first wave. We did not think it likely before, and we still don't think so, although Italy is trying its hardest to be admitted," said Klaus Friedrich, chief economist with Dresdner Bank.
To the annoyance of Italian politicians, bond and currency markets have in recent days been trading on the basis that Italy may not in the end make it into the first phase of EMU.

This has cancelled out some of the dramatic narrowing of the spread between yields on Italian and German government bonds over the past year on the expectation that Italy would in fact make it into EMU.

Italian politicians have been on the defensive following Wednesday's Financial Times article which quoted European monetary officials as saying Italy would be offered a face- saving deal to delay its entry into EMU until 2000 or 2001.

That plan, according to the article, would alleviate German fears that if Italy were among the first EMU members, the launch of a strong and stable single currency would be compromised and financial markets unsettled.

But there is also a risk if Italy stays outside currency union at the start, analysts said. A weakening lira would make Italian goods cheapers to export and thus make it difficult for French and German exporters to compete, they said.

Prodi said on the eve of his trip to Bonn that the concerns were unjustified and that Italy would meet all of the criteria for EMU membership as laid down in the Maastricht Treaty, the blueprint for currency union.
But most of the experts in the Reuters survey said Italy's bid to get into EMU from the start was almost certain to fail and that entry in a second wave by 2001 was more likely.
